Flamingos released

By: Sasha OLD | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Kamfersdam flamingo's have been released

Unique Selling Point:
49 baby flamingo's were released last week at Kampfersdam in Kimberley, Freestate. We will speak to Dr. Doug Harebottle, a Zoologist and head of the Sol-Plaatijie University's biology and land department. He will be monitoring and helping them re-integrate back in their original colony at the dam on a daily basis. There were over 2000 that were rescued in January and February, by numerous organizations - one of them was by bird lover and PI Mike Bolhuis. The dam had dried up and many birds had been abandoned by their parents - left to die from starvation and the heat. He and his team headed back to the dam now to release the wild flamingo's. Those Flamingo's that could not be re-wilded and became accustomed to humans, or developed subsequent diseases like "bid pox" and needed special care and attention were handed over to Lory Park Zoo's Zoologist Kara Heynis. NOBODY owns the flamingo's and there's been controversy over where those birds should go...

Press Release:


Flamingos Released
It’s been months since over 1600 lesser flamingo chicks were rescued from Kamfers Dam in Kimberley after the dam dried up, leaving hundreds abandoned and starving. Volunteers from around the country banded together to collect the newly hatched chicks, taking them to the local SPCA where they were fed and checked by a vet. Now, as they continue to recover, some baby flamingos are being released back into their natural habitat.
Producer: Sasha Schwendenwein
Presenter: Claire Mawisa


Script:


Kamfers dam outside of Kimberley in the Northern Cape, is home to 50,000 Lesser flamingos. But in February, instead of tending to their young, many birds abandoned their nests due to the pans dwindling water levels because of a lack of a municipal water, soaring temperatures and a prolonged drought.
LINK: Claire: “THIS IS WHAT A FLAMINGO NEST LOOKS LIKE NORMALLY THERE WOULD BE WATER HALFWAY UP THE NEXT AND THE FLAMINGO’S WOULD BE AROUND THE NEST, BUT BECAUSE THERE’S NO WATER, THE FLAMINGO’S ARE WAY OVER THERE…
As a result many chicks would hatch only to die. Instead of watching nature take its course, rescue organizations intervened saving around 1600 weak chicks by giving them medical attention, a good scrub and filling their empty belly’s.
UPSOUND: Claire: Am I messing all over you? I am…
Mike Bolhuis is a well-known security specialist, but many were surprised to learn his house in Pretoria North is a paradise for birds... including the flamingo.
Bolhuis: I immediately took action, I jumped the red tape and the legislations, got them on a plane and flew them here.
Four months ago, Bolhuis set up a temporary flamingo orphanage for roughly 900 dehydrated and frail chicks with the hope of releasing them back into the wild.
This month, now taller and stronger, the chicks were flown back to Kimberley. Ornithologist at Sol Plaatje University Dr. Doug Harebottle and his dedicated bird club volunteers are monitoring the NOW teenage birds.
Doc: “Once the birds get identified, we put on a metal ring onto the bird's leg the birds then get placed into a specially designed boxes, and transport it to the dam.”
Many birds were washed because when their oily food gets on their feathers, it hinders their own waterproofing. Then it was time for the release.
Bolhuis: “We released 49, there was 50 taken, one didn't want to go. We back and the next day they were 60 released and this Monday was we released another 59. It was it was a real emotional moment and when I saw them again with a release it just brought it all back. They’re really part of our lives and we really love.”
But, the reality is that about 200 chicks cannot be released back into the wild. Instead of euthanasia, they’re placed with various facilities that can cater to their special needs – like Lory Park Zoo in Gauteng. Zoologist Kara Heynis set up a temporary camp, away from visitors, to support the remaining sad cases like Philip and Susan who both caught bird pox.
Kara: “So it's a virus that we find naturally on the dam in the Flamingo flock but unfortunately it's become quite aggressive in the birds that were rescued. Phillip is unfortunately very human imprinted, he'll come running up to you and give you a cuddle, which means he's probably non releasable. He also has just received Pox surgery. So you'll see he's got some stitches on his forehead. And then, Susan was a pox bird who unfortunately hurt her hip during her recovery and now she's still in the process of physiotherapy.”
Heynis says the Pox birds may still be released, but only next season, while the non-releasable birds will go to the National Zoological gardens.
Kara: “It's been not without it’s heartache. But It's been an incredible four months of our lives.”
Since their release the birds are integrating successfully into the flock and some have been fitted with solar powered tracking devices.
Doc: “So part of the monitoring includes 20 birds that are being fitted with a G.P.S. transmitters. And those birds haven't been released yet they are still in the holding pen at the quarantine facility.”
Up to now it’s been uncertain where the Flamingos migrate to in the winter months, but the tracking devices will help all involved see their hard work realised.
